name: Overwatering
why: Constant saturation limits oxygen around roots, reducing their ability to take up water.
causes: Watering before soil has dried enough
Poor drainage or a pot that is too large
identification: Soil stays wet between waterings
Yellow leaves feel soft rather than crisp
recoverySteps: Feel soil below the surface before adding more water.
Empty the saucer and check drainage holes.
Let the mix dry to the depth recommended for this plant.
If stems are soft or roots smell unpleasant, inspect for rot.
Use fresh airy mix if the current mix stays waterlogged; reduce watering frequency.
prevention: Check soil rather than following a rigid calendar.
Use a draining pot and empty the outer cachepot.
recheck: Check soil in 2–3 days; assess new growth over 2–3 weeks.

name: Underwatering
why: Roots cannot supply leaves when the potting mix becomes too dry for the species.
causes: Heat, small pots, or root-bound growth
identification: Pot feels unusually light
Soil is dry below the surface; leaves feel crisp
recoverySteps: Check soil moisture through the root zone.
Water slowly and thoroughly until water drains.
If water runs around a dry root ball, soak the pot briefly, then drain fully.
Recheck leaf firmness the next day.
Adjust watering to the plant and room conditions.
prevention: Check moisture more often in warm weather.
Do not allow moisture-loving species to dry out completely.
recheck: Check in 24 hours and again after 3 days.

name: Root rot
why: Persistently wet, low-oxygen conditions favor organisms that damage root tissue.
causes: Blocked drainage or contaminated potting mix
identification: Roots are brown or black and mushy rather than firm
Root covering slips away; soil may smell unpleasant
recoverySteps: Gently remove the plant from its pot.
Inspect roots and trim only rotten, mushy parts using clean tools.
Clean tools between cuts and discard contaminated mix.
Repot in a clean draining pot with fresh suitable mix.
Water according to remaining roots and species needs; avoid saturation.
If the entire crown is rotten, recovery may not be possible; consider a healthy cutting.
prevention: Use well-aerated mix.
Avoid standing water and excessive pot sizes.
recheck: Inspect moisture in 2 days; watch for fresh growth over several weeks.

name: Yellowing leaves: investigate the cause
why: Yellowing is a sign, not a disease; leaf age, light, roots, and pests can all contribute.
causes: Water, light, nutrition, or pest stress
identification: Record whether one old leaf or many new leaves are affected
Compare moisture and light with the plant profile
recoverySteps: Inspect both sides of leaves and check soil moisture.
Separate normal shedding of a single old leaf from widespread yellowing.
Use the other possible causes below to guide inspection.
Correct the underlying condition; avoid removing every yellow leaf at once.
prevention: Track changes instead of making several care changes at once.
Check roots and lighting before adding fertilizer.
recheck: Inspect in 7 days; seek more clues if yellowing spreads.

name: Brown leaf tips: moisture or salt stress
why: Leaf tips may dry when water supply is uneven or salts accumulate in potting mix.
identification: Browning starts at tips or margins
White crust may be present on soil or the pot
recoverySteps: Check moisture and the room's humidity.
Pause fertilizer if salt buildup is visible.
If the pot drains freely, flush mix with low-mineral water and drain completely.
Trim only dead tips with clean scissors if desired.
prevention: Use diluted fertilizer only during growth.
Keep moisture consistent for the species.
recheck: Inspect new leaf tips after 2–3 weeks.

name: Spider mites
why: These tiny mites feed on leaf cells, producing fine pale speckling and sometimes webbing.
causes: Warm, dry conditions favor rapid multiplication
identification: Look for fine webbing and pinprick stippling
Tap a leaf over white paper and inspect moving specks
recoverySteps: Isolate the plant.
Rinse leaf undersides gently, protecting the soil from saturation.
Wipe leaves and remove heavily damaged foliage.
If needed, use a product labeled for mites on indoor plants; follow its label and patch-test.
Inspect nearby plants and repeat monitoring.
prevention: Inspect new plants before placing them nearby.
Keep leaves clean and avoid prolonged very dry air.
recheck: Inspect every 3–4 days for several weeks.

name: Mealybugs
why: Sap-feeding insects shelter in leaf joints and leave sticky honeydew.
identification: Cottony white clusters at leaf joints
Sticky residue without a powdery coating across the leaf
recoverySteps: Isolate the plant and inspect stems and leaf joints.
Remove visible insects with a damp swab.
Rinse or wipe accessible foliage.
For persistent colonies, choose a labeled indoor-plant insecticidal soap, patch-test, and follow directions.
Check nearby plants and remove recurring colonies.
prevention: Quarantine and inspect new arrivals.
Inspect leaf joints during routine cleaning.
recheck: Check weekly for at least a month.

name: Aphids
why: Small sap-feeding insects gather on tender new shoots and can distort emerging leaves.
identification: Clusters of pear-shaped insects on growing tips
Sticky honeydew and distorted young leaves
recoverySteps: Isolate the plant.
Wash aphids off with a gentle stream of water.
Prune a severely infested tip if appropriate.
Use a labeled indoor-plant soap only if needed, following all label directions.
Inspect new shoots for returning insects.
prevention: Check new growth regularly.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer.

name: Scale insects
why: Scale insects attach to stems or leaves and feed beneath protective covers.
causes: Insects overlooked on stems and leaf veins
identification: Fixed brown or tan bumps lift away from the leaf surface
Some species produce sticky honeydew
recoverySteps: Isolate the affected plant.
Gently remove accessible scales with a damp cloth.
Prune heavily infested growth when practical.
For persistent infestation, use a product labeled for scale on indoor plants, following its directions.
Inspect neighboring plants and repeat checks.
prevention: Inspect stems as well as leaf surfaces.
Keep new plants separate during initial observation.

name: Fungal leaf spots
why: Fungi can infect damp foliage, although similar spots can also have non-fungal causes.
causes: Leaves remaining wet for long periods
Poor air movement and contaminated debris
identification: Spots enlarge or develop halos over time
Pattern cannot be explained by a single burn or injury
recoverySteps: Separate the plant while you inspect it.
Remove badly affected leaves using clean tools.
Water soil directly and keep foliage dry.
Improve gentle air circulation without a cold draft.
If lesions continue spreading, seek a local horticultural diagnosis.
prevention: Avoid crowding and persistent leaf wetness.
Remove fallen leaves from the pot.
recheck: Photograph spots and compare in 5–7 days.

name: Powdery mildew
why: A fungal growth forms pale powdery patches; mineral deposits and mealybugs can look similar.
causes: Susceptible foliage in favorable humidity conditions
identification: Powdery patches spread across leaves
No cottony insects are found at leaf joints
recoverySteps: Isolate and check that the coating is not mineral residue.
Remove badly affected leaves with clean tools.
Improve spacing and gentle air movement.
Avoid improvised chemical mixtures; seek labeled plant-safe treatment advice if it spreads.
prevention: Avoid crowding plants.
Inspect new plants and maintain steady growing conditions.

name: Possible nutrient deficiency
why: A depleted mix or stressed roots can limit nutrients available for new growth.
identification: Growth is slow during the active season
Paling continues despite appropriate moisture and light
recoverySteps: Rule out root rot, low light, and pests first.
Check when the plant was last repotted or fed.
During active growth, use a balanced houseplant fertilizer at the label's appropriate diluted rate.
Do not fertilize a severely stressed plant with damaged roots.
prevention: Follow the plant profile's feeding guidance.
Refresh potting mix when needed rather than overfeeding.

name: Sunburn / excess light
why: Unacclimated leaves can scorch when exposed to strong direct sun.
causes: Sudden move to a sunny window
identification: Bleached or dry patches face the window
Damage follows a recent change of position
recoverySteps: Move into suitable filtered light.
Check moisture; do not automatically overwater.
Leave partly healthy leaves in place.
Acclimate slowly if the species can tolerate brighter exposure.
prevention: Use a sheer curtain for strong sun.
Change light exposure gradually.
recheck: Check in 3–5 days for new damage.

name: Low humidity
why: Dry indoor air increases leaf water loss, especially in humidity-loving plants.
identification: Tips brown despite appropriate soil moisture
New leaves may unfurl poorly
recoverySteps: Check humidity with a hygrometer if available.
Move away from heating and air-conditioning vents.
Use a clean humidifier to raise room humidity moderately.
Keep airflow and correct soil moisture; misting alone is short-lived.
prevention: Group compatible plants with space for airflow.
Avoid placing sensitive plants beside vents.

name: Cold damage
why: Cold temperatures damage tropical plant tissue and can slow root function.
causes: Cold drafts or contact with cold glass
identification: Damage appears after a cold night or move
Leaves develop dark, water-soaked patches
recoverySteps: Move to a stable temperature appropriate to the species.
Keep away from cold glass and drafts.
Wait until damage is clear before pruning dead tissue.
Check soil before watering because cold-stressed roots use less water.
prevention: Protect plants during transport.
Avoid sudden temperature swings.

name: Insufficient light
why: Too little usable light slows growth and causes plants to shed foliage they cannot support.
identification: New stems stretch toward light
New leaves are smaller and growth slows
recoverySteps: Move closer to a window with suitable indirect light.
Increase exposure gradually to prevent scorching.
Reduce watering frequency if growth remains slow.
Rotate periodically to encourage balanced growth.
prevention: Choose a position matching the species.
Reassess daylight as seasons change.

name: Natural aging of older leaves
why: Plants gradually recycle nutrients from older leaves as new leaves develop.
identification: Only one or a few oldest lower leaves change
New growth remains healthy; no spreading damage or pests
recoverySteps: Check roots, moisture, and pests before assuming normal aging.
Leave mostly green leaves attached.
Remove fully dead leaves with clean tools.
Continue normal care if growth remains healthy.
prevention: Observe the overall plant, not a single leaf.
Avoid unnecessary fertilizer or extra water.
recheck: Check in 1–2 weeks; widespread yellowing needs further inspection.

name: Chewing or mechanical damage
why: Irregular holes can come from chewing pests, pets, or physical injury; some species naturally have splits.
identification: New irregular holes differ from normal leaf shape
Look for pests, droppings, or a damaged emerging leaf
recoverySteps: Inspect both leaf surfaces and the pot at different times of day.
Separate the plant if an active pest is found.
Remove visible chewing pests safely.
Keep foliage clear of walkways and pets; damaged tissue will not regrow.
prevention: Inspect plants coming indoors.
Protect unfurling leaves from handling.
recheck: Check for fresh damage over the next 3–5 days.
